column1: What is the fixed DNS name format for a Kubernetes Service?

column2: Whether search domains are tried before querying a name as-is — fewer dots than 5 means search domains get tried first

column1: Why does a bare short service name fail across namespaces?
column2: The pod's search domains only include its OWN namespace — CoreDNS never even receives a query for the other namespace's version unless it's included explicitly

column1: Does the CoreDNS reload plugin validate a new Corefile before applying it?
column2: No — an invalid Corefile crashes CoreDNS on reload rather than being rejected gracefully

column1: Are Service environment variables always current?
column2: No — only injected for Services that existed before the pod started; DNS is always current by comparison

column1: Is dnsPolicy: Default actually the default policy?
column2: No, confusingly — ClusterFirst is the actual default; Default means the pod uses the NODE's DNS instead of CoreDNS

column1: What does dnsPolicy: None require that the other policies don't?
column2: A fully manual dnsConfig — nameservers, search domains, and options are all your own responsibility, nothing is injected automatically

column1: What problem does dnsPolicy: ClusterFirstWithHostNet solve?
column2: A pod running with hostNetwork: true would otherwise lose cluster-name resolution — this policy forces ClusterFirst-style behavior back on for that case

column1: A single Service name returns NXDOMAIN, but nslookup kubernetes.default works. What does that narrow down?
column2: CoreDNS itself is healthy — the problem is specific to that Service: wrong namespace, doesn't exist, or no Ready pods

column1: What's the blast radius when CoreDNS itself crashes vs. when a single Service is misconfigured?
column2: CoreDNS crashing breaks DNS resolution for the entire cluster simultaneously; a single Service misconfiguration only affects that one Service's name

column1: What CoreDNS plugin handles non-cluster DNS queries like google.com?
column2: forward — forwards them to the node's own /etc/resolv.conf

column1: What does the CoreDNS cache plugin do, and what's its default TTL for cluster DNS?
column2: Caches DNS responses to reduce repeated load on CoreDNS — 30 seconds by default in the standard Corefile

column1: What does the CoreDNS loadbalance plugin do?
column2: Randomizes the order of A/AAAA records in a response — this is the actual mechanism behind headless Services returning pod IPs in a different order each query
